newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-BORIS BLOWS AWAY BRIT BUT NO ONE MINDS MUCH.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-BORIS BLOWS AWAY BRIT BUT NO ONE MINDS MUCH.

text.p: Boris Becker beat a Briton at Wimbledon on Monday but the normally highly-partisan crowd did not mind a bit.
The 29-year-old German playing his 14th consecutive Wimbledon is something of an adopted son at the All England Club which he describes as his back yard.

After becoming the youngest champion as a 17-year-old, successfully defending his title a year later and winning again in 1989, Becker is one of the few players known universally by his first name -- like one of the family.
Even during mundane victories such as Monday's 6-3 6-3 6-2 stroll against Mark Petchey, Becker still produces moments of magic.
His first break of the Briton's serve in the second set involved a full length forehand dive and double roll on the grass, his racket flying from his hand. It was Boris of old and a winning shot.

Most of the time, perhaps mindful of his status as the most elderly seed in the draw, Becker has practised extreme economy of movement but he has still reached the fourth round without dropping a set.
On Monday he ran down only the rallies he really wanted to win and faced just one break point on his often deadly serve. He dismissed the point haughtily with an unreturnable serve and an ace.
"You never expect easy matches -- you take them if they come along but you always expect the worst," he said afterwards.
"I've been having a good time on my shots, on my serve. And I've been giving other players trouble all along from very early on in the matches," he added.
Becker believes he is the exception in winning Wimbledon so young, most others have been older and better able to withstand the psychological strains of a two-week tournament.
"You need to be very, very patient. Your nerves have to be excellent," he said. This has been particularly true this tournament with two days lost to rain and the schedule turned on its head.
Despite defaulting last year in the third round with a ruptured tendon and suffering a string of injury problems since, Becker feels he still has one Grand Slam left in him.
Petchey is convinced he can do it. "Boris is special...He's obviously got a chance of winning, there's no question," he said.
But Becker is in the tougher end of the draw and faces world number one Pete Sampras if both progress to the quarter-finals.
After Mondays's roars of delight when the smiling German flung his towels into the crowd then stopped to sign autographs, there is little doubt who would be the crowd's sentimental favourite.
